first_impression.reaction: My assistant shortlisted it because my fiance's family is Greek Orthodox and his mother has views on the church. The first screen is calm and serious: 'a sacrament, not a ceremony you write yourselves' sets the right tone. No exclamation marks, no packages, no price talk. Her summary: priest first, closed dates, two paperwork tracks, the Metropolis if we marry in Greece, and three resorts with their own Orthodox chapel. I read the Greece section, the chapel list and the close myself. The ceremony walkthrough I skimmed, because the priest and my mother-in-law will explain that.

journey.quote: Before you hold a venue or send a save-the-date, sit down with your parish priest, check that the Church can marry you, and check that your date is open.
journey.reaction: Sensible order, and said without fuss. Nobody is rushing me to book an island.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: A marriage cannot take place in the Orthodox Church between an Orthodox Christian and a non-Christian.
journey.reaction: Plainly stated, no softening. My assistant needs exactly this before anyone's time is wasted. If it applies to us, I'd rather know now.

journey.section: If one partner is not Orthodox
journey.quote: If a minister from the other partner's church is close to you, they can be welcomed as a guest, or invited to speak at the reception.
journey.reaction: Thoughtful about two families with different customs, without making a speech about it. That is the cultural awareness I look for.

journey.quote: In many Greek families the wedding sponsor is expected to baptise the first child, so choose with both roles in mind.
journey.reaction: This is the kind of family politics that causes real problems later. Useful, and not patronising.

journey.section: The Greek Orthodox wedding ceremony, step by step
journey.quote: Keep the train and the veil manageable for three slow turns.
journey.reaction: Fine for a bride doing this herself. My stylist will handle it. The whole step-by-step is long for me, but it is clear and my assistant skipped it.

journey.quote: It charges the Metropolis fee on top of its package.
journey.reaction: 'Package' again. It is the venue's word, not theirs, but it is the one line that sounds like standard wedding shopping.

journey.quote: Mykonos Grand states that both bride and groom must be Christian Orthodox to hold a religious wedding on the hotel premises.
journey.reaction: A house rule I would never have guessed. Stated as a fact, no commentary. Good.

journey.quote: Nana Princess in Crete holds Greek Orthodox weddings in its private Chapel of St George.
journey.reaction: Private chapel is the phrase my assistant highlighted. A chapel inside the property is the only way I can see the church service staying out of public view.

journey.quote: A venue chapel keeps everyone in one place, from the ceremony to the last toast.
journey.reaction: Yes. One perimeter, one security plan. Costa Navarino with two chapels is where my mind goes first.

journey.quote: On Paros, the municipality names Panagia Ekatontapiliani and a string of country chapels as favourite wedding churches, with guests arriving by boat, carriage or on foot with musicians.
journey.reaction: Romantic, and impossible for us. A procession through a village is a photograph on someone's phone within the hour.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: **Guest numbers.** How many people fit inside the church, and where do the rest stand?
journey.reaction: The right question, and the one that matters most to us at 300 guests. But it is left for me to ask. The page doesn't say whether any of these chapels holds more than a handful.

journey.section: Questions to ask the priest and the venue
journey.quote: **Photography and video.** Where may the photographer stand during the crowning, and is flash allowed?
journey.reaction: Good, but for me the question is the opposite one: who else is allowed to photograph, and can guests' phones be kept out of the church.

journey.section: Plan your Greek Orthodox wedding with Wedded Concierge
journey.quote: Your priest settles the service. Everything around it, from the island and the chapel to the guests' flights and the long lunch after, is ours to plan.
journey.reaction: Understated and confident. It knows its place next to the Church, which my future in-laws will respect.

unanswered_questions: Which of these chapels (St George at Nana Princess, St Samson or St Eleni at Costa Navarino, Grecotel Mykonos Lolita) can seat a large family, and how are 200 to 400 guests handled when the church is small?
Can a resort with its own chapel be closed to other guests for the wedding and the days around it?
Can phones and outside photography be controlled during the service, and can our security team work with the venue's and the church's?
If we marry in Greece but live between Dubai, Sydney and London, which priest and which Metropolis do we start with?
Have they planned an Orthodox wedding at this scale in Greece, and is there a private or referral route to someone senior?

turn_offs_found.quote: It charges the Metropolis fee on top of its package.
turn_offs_found.why: Package language puts me back among standard clients, which is one of my fears. It is reported venue wording and appears once, so it is a nudge, not a deal-breaker.

would_share_with: My assistant, to ask Costa Navarino and Nana Princess about chapel capacity and closing the property
My fiance's mother, for the koumbaros point and the closed dates
Our family office, for the Greece paperwork order and the Metropolis approval timing

cta_reaction.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, and confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
cta_reaction.why: The close is quiet and 'anywhere in the world' reads better for a family across three countries. But I don't fill in web forms, and nothing here shows they think at 300 guests. Through my assistant or a referral, possibly.

top_3_changes: Next to the guest numbers question, add one short line on what happens when the family is larger than the chapel (for example the service inside, the wider family outside or on the grounds, confirmed with the priest and venue), so a large-family reader sees her situation acknowledged.

Add a privacy line to the photography and venue chapel points, such as asking the priest and venue about guest phones and outside photography during the service, which fits the existing 'Questions to ask' list without new claims.
Rephrase the Elounda sentence so it doesn't end on 'package' (for example 'It charges the Metropolis fee separately'), keeping the fact intact.
